title: A Water Bottle and the Boston Strangler
central_question: How did a thrown-away water bottle link the confessed Boston Strangler to one murder, and what does it not prove?
content_notes: 40-second cut of Case File 16. Closed historical case. DeSalvo confessed but was never tried for the stranglings; the 2013 DNA evidence links him to Mary Sullivan's murder ONLY, and the narration says that whether he killed all thirteen women is still debated. The hook headline reads 'A thrown-away water bottle and the Boston Strangler' and claims nothing more. DeSalvo appears only as an anonymous silhouette with no likeness. The nephew whose discarded water bottle was collected is never named or shown (a small generic silhouette stands in on a generic street); the DeSalvo family's objection is on screen. Victims are never depicted and no method is described; Mary Sullivan is named respectfully because the DNA result concerns her case and her family welcomed it. The cemetery is a generic wide dawn shot with no coffin or remains. No real photograph, police, court or DA material, logo, newspaper or document is imitated; the bottle is a plain generic bottle. No dialogue is invented. Status verified 2026-10-12.

lines.text: A man confessed to being the Boston Strangler.
From 1962 to 1964, thirteen women were killed around Boston.
That man, Albert DeSalvo, was never tried for them.
Decades later, detectives secretly followed one of his nephews.
He threw away a water bottle. They took it.
Its DNA was a familial match to evidence from Mary Sullivan's case.
To be sure, they exhumed DeSalvo's remains.
Officials said it left no doubt he killed Mary Sullivan.
But it links him to her murder only.
Whether he killed all thirteen is still debated.
For Mary Sullivan's family, the answer started with a thrown-away water bottle.

claims.text: Thirteen women were killed in and around Boston between 1962 and 1964 in the killings attributed to the 'Boston Strangler'. (Some reports count 11 or 14; 13 is the most common count.) No victim other than Mary Sullivan is named; no method is described.

In 1965, while already in custody on other charges, Albert DeSalvo confessed to the Strangler killings (to a psychiatrist and, through his lawyer F. Lee Bailey, in tape-recorded sessions with investigators).

For decades many doubted the confession: no physical evidence tied him to the killings, critics argued he could have learned the details elsewhere, he later recanted, and Mary Sullivan's nephew wrote a book arguing he was not her killer.
DeSalvo was never tried (never charged) for any of the Strangler killings, for lack of physical evidence.
Mary Sullivan, 19, killed in Boston in January 1964, is considered the last (final) victim. She is named only, never depicted.

Detectives (a Boston Police fugitive-squad detective) secretly followed DeSalvo's male relatives until one, a nephew who was not named at the news conference, drank from and threw away a water bottle, which the detective took. No source found gives the date of the collection, so the narration says only 'decades later'. The relative is never named or shown in this episode.

DNA from the bottle was a 'familial' (Y-chromosome) match to evidence from the Sullivan case, announced on 11 July 2013; the DA called it strong but not enough on its own to close the case with absolute certainty, and sought DeSalvo's exhumation.

DeSalvo's remains were exhumed (court-ordered, July 2013) and his DNA tested; on 19 July 2013 officials announced a match (odds of another white male put at one in 220 billion), and Attorney General Martha Coakley said it 'leaves no doubt' that he was responsible for Mary Sullivan's murder.
The DNA links DeSalvo to Mary Sullivan's murder only; authorities said no DNA survives from the other cases, and whether one man (DeSalvo) committed all the killings is still debated.

Casey Sherman, Mary Sullivan's nephew, who had long argued DeSalvo was innocent, accepted the 2013 result and called it 'full justice for my aunt'; DA Dan Conley said questions Mary's family had asked for almost 50 years had been answered. (Basis for 'For Mary Sullivan's family, the answer started with a thrown-away water bottle'.)
DeSalvo's family, through lawyer Elaine Sharp, disputed the conclusion and objected to the covert collection of a relative's DNA; DA Conley called the method fair, legal and ethical.

NEXT CASE card (no narration): in December 2022 FBI agents collected trash the Kohberger family set out at their Pennsylvania home; DNA from it indicated the father of the person whose DNA was on a knife sheath at the Idaho crime scene. Bryan Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 and was sentenced to four consecutive life terms.
